I am a 45-year-old woman farmer in Quzhou County. I have been farming this land since I was young, and my family has about 8 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. My husband works part-time in the county town, and I take care of the fields with help from my elderly father-in-law. I only finished primary school, but I know this land well. I do not take risks with new crops that I am not sure about. Around here, we grow what we know, and what the grain station will buy.

My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October after the National Day holiday, using the seed I saved from last year mixed with some new improved seed my neighbor recommended. It looks green and healthy now. I will irrigate it three or four more times before harvest in early June: the green-up water, the jointing water, the heading water, and maybe one more if the spring is too dry. I will topdress urea when it starts jointing, because wheat is hungry then. I also need to spray for aphids and weeds, and maybe fungus if the weather turns humid. After I harvest the wheat in June, I will burn the stubble back into the field and plant maize straight away — no ploughing, just direct seeding with the machine. Everyone here uses Denghai 605 hybrid maize now; the seed is expensive but the yield is good and the grain dealer pays well for it. Maize needs less water than wheat — two good irrigations, one when it is knee-high and one at tasseling, should be enough. I will fertilize at planting and maybe side-dress once when it is growing fast. I need to watch for armyworms and corn borers, so I will spray insecticide two or three times, and once for weeds. If the weather is kind, I should get over 1,000 jin per mu for both crops, which is enough to feed my family and sell the rest to pay for my child's school fees.

I do not grow cotton or vegetables on my main land — that is too much labor and too risky. Wheat and maize are safe. The government gives a small subsidy for wheat, and I can always sell maize to the local buyer. This is how my family has always done it, and I see no reason to change.

Wheat is sown in October and harvested in June; maize follows immediately in the same field through no-tillage direct seeding and is harvested by October. I use improved wheat varieties saved from previous years and hybrid maize seed (like Denghai 605) purchased from the local dealer because it gives the best yield. I apply compound fertilizer as a basal dose and topdress nitrogen during the growing season. Wheat needs more irrigation (4 times) and pesticide applications (4 times including insecticide, herbicide, and fungicide) than maize (2 irrigations and 3 pesticide applications). Rotary tillage before wheat sowing and no-tillage for maize are the standard practices in my village, saving labor and fuel while maintaining yield.
